results.summary: This project is a small UART-driven ALU processor implemented in Verilog. It receives three bytes over UART (opcode, operand A, operand B), computes the result with an 8-bit ALU, and returns the result byte over UART. The UART protocol is 8N1 at 115200 baud with a 50 MHz clock. Testing involves connecting a UART adapter to uio[0] and uio[1], sending three bytes, and reading back the result byte.

results.summary: This project is an experimental GF180 submission of raybox-zero, a framebuffer-less VGA display generator that implements a simple 3D-like ray casting game engine. It is inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, using a grid of wall blocks with textured walls that can be internally generated or read from off-chip QSPI memory, plus optional sliding doors and flat-coloured floor and ceiling. The player POV registers and other visual effects are controlled through a single SPI interface. It outputs a standard VGA 640x480@59.94Hz signal on the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a clock around 25.175 MHz.

results.summary: This project is a Verilog demo submitted to the TT10 demo competition, containing a logo, star field, twister, and spiralling balls. It includes a floating point unit used for the twister and spiralling balls, plus a synthesizer and sequencer. The video output is VGA 640x480@60Hz clocked at 50.4 MHz, giving two clock cycles per pixel. Testing requires a TinyVGA-compatible Pmod and Mike's audio Pmod, with all inputs set to zero for default behavior.

results.summary: This project is a SystemVerilog test for an 8b10 serializer/deserializer, containing an 8b10 encoder and decoder. Nine-bit symbols can be pushed in and results pop out a number of clocks later. The manual clock is divided by 10 to generate internal clocks, and both transmitter and receiver use handshake strobes on the bidirectional pins. Testing involves setting up a manual clock, sending the COM character, waiting for link lock on uio[7], and checking that received characters match what was sent.

results.summary_before: This design generates a VGA video signal that animates columns of pink hearts transitioning on and off the screen. It is implemented in Verilog using the VGA Playground environment and is intended to be tested by running the simulation and observing the output. The design requires a VGA monitor connected to the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. The project is a playful visual demonstration rather than a practical application.
results.summary: This design is a Verilog melody generator that uses two Markov chains, one for note selection and one for note duration, on a pentatonic scale. An LFSR generates two 8-bit pseudorandom numbers that drive the Markov chain transitions, and two FSMs model the chains while a PWM generator outputs the target note. Inputs allow selecting one of sixteen melodies via the last four seed bits, plus adjustable BPM and duration matrix selection. A buzzer PMOD is required to hear the generated melodies.
